products.name: Shopify
products.key_insight: Shopify shows how behavioral design can serve both platform and user goals simultaneously. The setup wizard uses progressive commitment, but the merchant genuinely gets a working store. The $1 trial uses anchoring, but the merchant genuinely gets to test the platform risk-free. The app ecosystem creates lock-in, but it also creates genuine value. This alignment between behavioral technique and user outcome is what separates ethical persuasion from manipulation.

products.name: Airbnb
products.key_insight: Airbnb's design is a masterclass in reducing the trust barrier of the sharing economy — reviews, verified photos, and Superhost badges genuinely solve the 'sleeping in a stranger's home' problem. But the same product that innovated trust also deploys classic conversion dark patterns: manufactured scarcity, fee hiding, and price anchoring. The tension between 'design that builds trust' and 'design that maximizes conversion' is visible in every booking flow. Airbnb's ethical score is middling precisely because it excels at both genuine value creation and subtle manipulation.

products.name: Amazon
products.key_insight: Amazon is the most commercially successful behavioral design in history — and the most ethically polarized. One-click buy genuinely reduces friction. Prime genuinely provides value. But the same behavioral toolkit that makes buying easy makes canceling hard. Amazon proves that behavioral design is morally neutral: identical techniques (friction manipulation, default exploitation, cognitive load management) create user value when applied to purchasing and destroy user autonomy when applied to retention. The regulatory response (FTC lawsuit, EU DSA) suggests that the market is beginning to price in behavioral design ethics.
